title: An Interview with Jerry Kvale: Faith Through Dementia
speaker: Jerry Kvale
summary: Jerry Kvale shares his personal testimony of meeting his wife Alana, their early married life and Christian walk, and their journey through her Alzheimer's diagnosis and 12.5-year decline. The interview focuses on how faith in Christ sustained the family through this trial, emphasizing God's faithfulness, the importance of keeping marriage vows, and practical ways the church can minister to families affected by dementia.

outline.title: Meeting and Early Marriage
subpoints: Met Alana at a birthday party in 1967 while in college
Married February 15, 1969 in a Valentine's Day wedding
Naval service during Vietnam War created early marital challenges
Started family with daughters Deanna (1971) and Colleen (1975)
Active in church life and Bible study through the 1970s and 1980s

outline.title: The Alzheimer's Diagnosis
subpoints: Alana diagnosed with Alzheimer's in 2009 after behavioral changes and memory loss
Diagnosis was devastating for the family
Jerry struggled with wanting to fix the problem himself
Quit his 37-year forestry career with DNR in 2010 to care for Alana at home

outline.title: The Spiritual Journey Through Caregiving
subpoints: Learned to love wife sacrificially through Ephesians 5:25 on Christ's love for the church
Recognized his idolatry problem of trying to fix things instead of trusting God
Discovered God's faithfulness through daily reminder 'she's in his hands'
Learned spiritual lessons about prayer through wife's incoherent communication

outline.title: Transition to Assisted Living
subpoints: Wife's behavior became increasingly aggressive and dangerous after 3 years at home
Church member's daughter worked in long-term care and connected family with Brookdale assisted living
Alana placed in Brookdale facility where she received excellent care for 12.5 years
Jerry visited daily, spending several hours at the facility

outline.title: God's Faithfulness Through the Trial
subpoints: God proved faithful in providing excellent care and protection for Alana
Realized Alana's aggressive behavior was not her fault
Comforted by knowing she is now in her right mind with the Lord
Total journey from diagnosis to death was 17 years

outline.title: Ministry to Families with Dementia
subpoints: Remember that dementia is not the person's fault
Love and accept people with dementia as image-bearers of God
Go with the flow of their changing topics and communication
The primary caregiver suffers most and needs respite care
Volunteer to sit with the patient to give spouse a break
Assisted living or professional care may become necessary
Trust God's provision and care rather than relying on human solutions

outline.title: Life After Loss
subpoints: Alana passed away, now with the Lord
Jerry praising God that she is no longer in pain or humiliation
Finding new purpose and adjusting to the wide-open schedule
Spending more time in prayer and seeking God's direction

transcript:
## Opening Scripture

> Therefore, we do not lose heart. Even though our outward man is perishing, yet the inward man is being renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, is working for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. While we do not look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporary, but the things which are not seen are eternal. (2 Corinthians 4:16-18)

## Meeting and Early Marriage

Where did you meet your wife?

A little bit of history. I graduated from high school in 1966 and she graduated in 1967 from Lincoln in Tacoma. I had just finished my first year at Tacoma Community College. I was beginning to pursue a forestry degree and she had just graduated from high school. We happened to meet at a birthday party for a mutual acquaintance. It was kind of romantic. You walk into the room and across the room, I saw this pretty young girl. It was kind of like our eyes just locked. I chased her until she caught me.

Were you both following the Lord at that time?

I don't know about Alana. She attended the Lutheran Church in Tacoma and her grandmother was a great Christian who loved to take her to church and read the Bible all the time. But she came from a dysfunctional family, so there wasn't a lot of church training in that family. Her mom went to church too with her grandmother, and that was kind of the extent of it. For me, I was attending the Bible Presbyterian Church in Tacoma.

What year is that again?

1967 is when we met. So I started taking her to church. That's the only thing I knew to do with girls back then. I was a farm boy and I didn't know how to work with girls, but it worked.

And then you got married in?

We had a long dating period. We met in 1967 and got married on February 15th, 1969. My wife wanted a Valentine's wedding in the worst way, but the Tacoma Bible Presbyterian Church had already scheduled a Valentine's banquet. So our wedding got pushed to the 15th, but she always told everybody we got married on Valentine's Day.

### Early Years and Naval Service

Before we got married, I joined the Naval Reserves because back then was the Vietnam War and I was eligible to be drafted into the Army to go to Vietnam. So I joined the Naval Reserves and did weekend training. Then in April, after we got married in February, I was called to active duty. I had to spend two years on a ship.

What kind of ship was that?

It was a destroyer based in Tacoma. It was a reserve trainer, but it wasn't home much. Every weekend we'd take off or go on two-week cruises. We were constantly training other reserves, so we weren't home a lot. We spent time in San Diego and Alaska, and I got to go to Hawaii. It was hard on our married life at first because we weren't growing together very well. But her family and my family watched over her and took care of her, so she wasn't totally alone.

### Building a Family and Church Life

After I got out of the Navy in 1971, I finished my schooling and got a job in Shelton, Washington. In 1971, our oldest daughter, Deanna, was born, and our second daughter, Colleen, was born in 1975 in Shelton. While we were there, we started attending the First Baptist Church. Since we had been attending the Bible Presbyterian Church, we looked hard for a Presbyterian church, but we didn't have any there.

During that time, we had a really good Christian walk with the Lord. My wife had never really professed her witness as knowing Christ, but she sure exhibited it in her prayer life and in her Bible reading and study. We talked a lot and prayed a lot together. There wasn't a particular time when I knew for certain she was a Christian, but she professed to know all the right things.

It was a good church. We had a good family life with our brothers and sisters there. She was quite involved with women's fellowship and prayer groups. I was with the men's groups. I led a home Bible discipleship program for about 12 years. Every week we would have family meetings. We were part of a youth group. She was a very submissive wife, pretty submissive. She was quiet and didn't like to talk the way I do.

### Daughters Remember Her Faith

Colleen, what do you remember about the faith of your mother?

It was a simple faith, but I remember many nights going to bed. My dad read his Bible in the morning at the kitchen table before work. It was a great example for us. But my mom was not a morning person, so she did hers at night. I would often go to bed and she'd be sitting at the table reading her Bible.

## The Alzheimer's Diagnosis

We don't have a particular date that dementia started showing up, and that's quite normal with anyone who's had dementia in the family. Funny habits started to develop. Memory loss wasn't the big one, but it was certainly part of it as things progressed. Alana and I thought there was something wrong, so she started seeing a physician to help determine what it was. Finally, the physician diagnosed her with Alzheimer's in 2009.

### Learning of the Diagnosis

You've been married now for about 40 years at that point. Then when the diagnosis was known, that must have been very devastating. Were you with her at the doctor's office?

Yes, I was with her. The doctor did the normal testing two or three times, and finally he said, looking right at her, "You have Alzheimer's." It was just a shock to her system. I think she was fearing that. I remember her mother used to joke about Alzheimer's all the time. She called it "Old Timer's Disease." And so now Alana had it.

Other Family Members Share Their Experiences

Kathy, when you and David found out that he had dementia—a different kind of dementia—how was that experience?

He did not have memory issues either, but odd behaviors that we were questioning. Our family doctor referred us to a neuropsychologist, and they did testing on him for a full day. Then they called me in and said they had good news and bad news. The good news was that he didn't have Alzheimer's, but they suspected some sort of dementia.

How did that affect you when you found out it was dementia?

I think you have no idea unless you've known someone who's walked through it. You have no idea exactly where that's going to go. We learned many things over the next 17 years that I wish we knew in the beginning.

Jim, how did you find out your wife had dementia?

Well, it was a long process. In 2008, we moved away from the Tri-Cities to Spokane to be closer to family, and one of the reasons I wanted to move there was because I sensed something was going wrong with my wife's memory. But it was another six or seven years before we had a firm diagnosis. It wasn't just memory loss, but also loss of motion on the left side and a lot of pain.

How did that affect you spiritually?

It was scary, but in the long run it drew me much closer to the Lord as I began to rely more and more on him.

Renee, you also lost your husband to dementia. How did that come about?

Well, he had Alzheimer's, and his father also suffered from Alzheimer's, so it was genetic. He went through the same series of testing that Alana did, and it was determined pretty early that he had Alzheimer's. It was really a hard disease because you slowly watch someone disappear and become something different.

## The Journey of Caregiving

### Quitting Work to Care at Home

One of the things she exhibited was the fact that she didn't want to be alone. I was still working with the state in a regular job, but I could see right away she was really deteriorating. I figured I'm going to stay home and take care of her, not knowing that this was going to be the beginning of a long road.

In 2010, a year after she was diagnosed, I quit a job that I loved and took care of her for the next three years. I had put 37 years in with the Department of Natural Resources in forestry.

### The Personality Changes

During that time, she deteriorated. Her personality changed 100%. She used to be a sweet, loving, quiet, very loving person, and all of that changed. She got to the point where she became very aggressive and antagonistic and confused. It was not fun. I had to start worrying about my own safety.

How are you dealing with that in your relationship with the Lord during that time?

It was hard because you keep asking yourself, "Lord, what's going on?" You don't know. But the Lord kept bringing up Ephesians 5:25 to me. He kept telling me, "You've got to love your wife. Husbands, love your wife like Christ loved the church." I didn't know what that meant, but I learned over the next many years.

When I finally shared this before—and I know it's kind of funny, but it's not—I said, "But Lord, you've never been married." The Holy Spirit reminded me very quickly, "Yeah, I'm married. I'm married to the church, and I love the church. I demonstrated that." So I said, "Okay, I'll do that." And he gave me the help to do it, the strength, and consistency.

Then I remembered my marriage vow: "Through sickness and health, till death do we part." He reminded me, "You made that promise to me back in 1969. I also made it to the church and to your wife. Don't forget that you made a promise to all of us that you would keep that." That kept me there. And it's really neat because I learned how to love her better through all of that. I think that's what God wanted me to learn.

### The Move to Assisted Living

Yes, I got to the point where I could not have her in the home anymore. I called the doctor and he said, "Get her over to St. Pete's right away. They have a ward to take care of psychotic people." So I took her there.

To make a long story short, the psychiatrist there said, "What do you want to do with her?" I said, "I want to get her healed and take her home." He said, "Most people when they're like this say, 'You take her.'" He was prepared to take her and put her in Western State or someplace like that, and I wouldn't even have a choice.

That's when I shared this with my Bible study and Sunday school class at Westwood. She was there five days. Within three days, they put her in the psychiatric ward, and a guy in our Bible study class said, "My daughter works in long-term care. Would you like to talk to her?" I said, "Sure." She came and met me at the hospital. I explained to her what I wanted to do, and she said, "Let me go talk to the psychiatrist." She went and talked to the psychiatrist and convinced him to let me try to put her in an assisted living home. Two days later, she was at Brookdale, and they accepted her in her violent condition.

### The Moment of Release

How was your heart when your wife was no longer living at home with you, but in a facility?

Well, the first night I remember after I left the psychiatric ward, I went home and I fell on my knees before the Lord. I said, "I realized that I had an idolatry problem. I was putting my faith in myself to fix her and in doctors. I said, 'There has got to be a doctor somewhere that can fix this.'" And he said, "No, just trust me. I'm the physician." So I said, "Okay, Lord, I give her back to you." And I did.

I felt a special peace right then, knowing that she was now in his hands. In fact, I wrote a great big sign on my refrigerator that said "She's in his hands." One of my granddaughters actually made a plaque that says that, so now I can hang it on the wall. That's what I did over the next 12 years. I kept reminding myself, "She's in your hands. Thank you for letting me come and see her."

### Living with an Unresponsive Wife

So tell us about 12 years, mostly of an unresponsive wife. Is it fair to say?

Yeah. She could communicate for the first couple of years, but it was kind of incoherent. I didn't even know if I could pray or read the Bible to her because she didn't make sense. But after a while, I did anyway, and a whole lot more toward the end, I would pray with her. She couldn't respond.

But there was one humorous thing that I wrote in my blog notes. I had a brother-in-law, John Pribill, who also had Alzheimer's. When they were together, they could kind of talk and mumble to each other, and they'd seem like they knew what they were talking about, but nobody else knew. So she would try to talk to me and explain things, but it was frustrating that she couldn't.

I got to the point where I said, "You know, this is just like me in my prayer life. Sometimes I try to tell God what my problem is or what I want to tell him, and I don't know how to say it to him." He said, "Yeah, Jerry, that's how your prayer life is." But thank goodness God gave me the Holy Spirit to interpret for me. God hears what my heart is saying, even if I don't know what to say. I've remembered that the whole time.

## Life After Alana's Passing

### Processing the Loss

So 12 and a half years, and she now passes and is with the Lord. How are you now?

I'm still trying to figure that out. I would go visit her every day. That was about half my day because I drive up from Centralia, spend a couple of hours with her, and sometimes I'd work at the mission to fill the rest of the day. But that whole gap is now wide open, visiting her. I'm still at the point of figuring out what's next.

First of all, I'm praising God that she's in her right mind. She gets to worship with him in person. And that's a comfort to me. Because she's not in pain, she's not suffering, she's not humiliated. My wife was a very modest lady, and now for 12 years to have somebody bathe her, dress her, take her to the bathroom, feed her—that had to be very humiliating if she was aware of it. I think she was for part of it.

So I'm still looking for what the Lord would like me to do to fill that blank time. Right now I'm trying to get through the memorial service. That's my focus at the moment, and it takes up a lot of time. But at the same time, I'm beginning to have more time to stop and just think about the Lord. I do a lot more praying now.

### Duration of the Journey

If I've kept the dates straight in my mind, it's about 17 years from diagnosis to death.

Kathy, how long was that for you?

Nine.

Jim, how long was that for you?

Ten years.

Renee, how long was that for you?

Seven years.

## Ministry to Families with Dementia

Just briefly, how can a church, the body of Christ, minister to a family going through a family member struggling with dementia?

Okay, that's easy. And you also asked the question, "How can you minister to people with dementia?" The answer is keep in mind one thing: People who have dementia—it's not their fault. When my wife was acting out against me, it wasn't her fault. I realized that. I wish I would have known it at the time, but I didn't. I know that now, and I'd like to pass that on to anybody who has family members doing that, if they get to that point.

The second thing is: Treat them and love them the way they're created in God's image. After all, just love them, accept them. You can joke with them, talk to them. Just go with the flow. Their subjects may change every minute, but that's okay. Just go with it.

### Caring for the Primary Caregiver

Now the church—the people who suffer the most are generally the spouses taking care of the person with dementia. They're willing to do it, but it's very tiring. It's a 24-7 job. You can't sleep. I even had to put a baby monitor in my bedroom to see if my wife got up in the middle of the night to wander. So it never stops. You're always on the edge, and you get exhausted.

So give them a break. If you know them, go volunteer to sit with that person so they can go out shopping or spend four or five hours visiting other people. They need the break.

### Long-term Care Options

If they eventually get to the part where they can't take care of them anymore, of course, they're going to have to find a way to put them in a rest home or a nursing home or some kind of assisted living. Unless the Lord changes plans and has something else, you can quite often take care of them at home by bringing caregivers in. There's a whole bunch of different ways to do it, but it generally depends on your income level because it's not cheap.

But the Lord, I have to say this: Every day of my 12 years there, my wife was taken care of very well. That was God being faithful to his promise. He said, "I'll take care of her." Every day she was loved and taken care of better than I could have. And so I have to praise him for that because he didn't forsake us. He didn't leave us. He just gave me a different way of life to look at her and to see what his plan is.

We have our plans, but he has his plans too. This is a great note for us to stop on—God's great faithfulness.

## Closing Prayer

Our precious God and great Heavenly Father, I'd like to thank you, dear God, for being the faithful God that we've just been talking about. We thank you, Lord, that you've never forsaken us or given us up. You're always there, especially when we ask. I just want to praise your name for that. Lord, I just pray that you'll be with each one of us and may we remember the blessings you've promised us, and especially that one day we will get to see you face to face. Thank you for that and for that promise. In the name of your son, Jesus, I pray. Amen.
